common_name: Raspberry Wine Bee Balm (Deep Pink-Red Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raspberry Wine spreads by underground stolons and benefits from division every two to three years to keep the colony within bounds.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew. Raspberry Wine produces large, shaggy clusters of deep magenta-pink flowers in midsummer above aromatic, mint-scented foliage, drawing hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies in large numbers over a long bloom period. It shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older bee balm cultivars, a disease that commonly disfigures monarda foliage by midsummer in humid climates, though good spacing and airflow still help keep plants looking their best. Divide every two to three years in spring to control its spreading habit and maintain vigorous, healthy growth.

common_name: Tomato Soup Coneflower (Vivid Red Double-Layered Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tomato Soup produces vivid, saturated red flowers, a bold departure from the purple-pink of the wild species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Tomato Soup is a modern coneflower cultivar bred for intensely saturated, brick-red flowers with broad, slightly overlapping petals surrounding a coppery-orange central cone, a bold, warm color unlike the softer purple-pinks of the wild species. It blooms over a long summer season, draws butterflies and bees, and holds its color well in the heat rather than fading, though like many of the newer colorful coneflower hybrids it can be somewhat shorter-lived than straight Echinacea purpurea in humid climates, benefiting from excellent drainage. Leaving spent seed heads standing through winter provides food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

common_name: Hot Papaya Coneflower (Double Orange-Red Pompom Echinacea)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hot Papaya produces fully double, pompom-like flowers in warm orange-red tones, quite different from the flat, single daisy form of the wild species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Hot Papaya is a striking double-flowered coneflower cultivar, producing dense, shaggy, pompom-like blooms that transition from a fiery orange-red center to a softer orange-gold at the petal tips, an ornamental, almost dahlia-like form quite different from the simple single daisy flowers typical of wild coneflowers. Its unusual double form makes it a strong focal point in a mixed border and an excellent cut flower, though like other novelty double coneflower cultivars it can be somewhat shorter-lived than the species and benefits from sharp drainage, particularly through humid summers. It still attracts pollinators, though double flowers generally offer less accessible pollen and nectar than single-flowered types.

planting.note: Surface sow, as the seed needs light; Cappuccino blooms the first year from an early start, producing warm mahogany-brown flowers ringed in gold, a distinctive departure from the solid yellow of the classic wild black-eyed Susan.

directions: Surface sow in well-drained, average soil in full sun, since the fine seed needs light to germinate well. Cappuccino produces richly colored flowers with a warm mahogany-brown center zone bordered by a bright golden-yellow edge, a striking bicolor combination that stands out among the many solid-yellow black-eyed Susan cultivars available. Grown as a short-lived perennial or reseeding annual depending on climate, it blooms heavily from summer into fall and makes an excellent cut flower, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its bloom period. Deadheading spent flowers extends the bloom season, and leaving a few seed heads to mature late in the season allows it to self-sow for the following year.

common_name: Tutti Frutti Agastache (Vivid Raspberry-Pink Anise Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Tutti Frutti requires excellent drainage, since it is prone to rot in heavy, wet clay or standing water, particularly through humid Gulf South summers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; raised beds or amended soil help ensure the sharp drainage this plant needs. Tutti Frutti produces tall, dense spikes of vivid raspberry-pink flowers over aromatic, licorice-scented foliage from summer into fall, drawing hummingbirds and bees in large numbers over its long bloom season. Like other hyssop hybrids it is somewhat shorter-lived in humid, high-rainfall climates than in drier regions, and excellent drainage is the single most important factor in getting it to persist for more than a season or two. Deadheading spent spikes encourages continued flowering, and the aromatic foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits.
